question_text: Solve dy/dx + y sec x = tan x.

insider_note: The integrating factor here is sec x + tan x, not the plain sec x that appears in the three neighbouring questions — that difference alone is worth double-checking, since it is easy to reuse the wrong I.F. from a nearby answer on the same page.

steps.label: Identify P and find ∫P dx
steps.margin_note: One mark. The equation is already in the standard linear form; P is the coefficient of y, which is sec x here.
steps.memory_tip: ∫sec x dx = log|sec x + tan x| — a standard integral, worth memorising on its own.
lines: Given D.E is in the form dy/dx + yP(x) = Q(x).
This is a linear D.E in y.
⇒ ∫P dx = ∫sec x dx = log|sec x + tan x|
steps.why: Reading P off the standard linear form here gives sec x, not tan x as in the neighbouring questions, and its integral is a separate standard result that must be recalled correctly.
common_mistakes: Confusing this P = sec x with the P = tan x seen in the three surrounding questions on the same page.
Writing ∫sec x dx as log(sec x) instead of the correct log|sec x + tan x|.

steps.label: Find the integrating factor
steps.margin_note: One mark. I.F. = e^(∫P dx) always.
steps.memory_tip: e^(log|sec x + tan x|) = sec x + tan x — the log and exponential cancel directly.
lines: ∴ I.F. = e^(∫P dx) = e^(log|sec x + tan x|)
steps.why: Applying the integrating-factor formula to the ∫P dx found in step 1 gives sec x + tan x, since the exponential undoes the log exactly as in every other linear equation.
common_mistakes: Writing the I.F. as just sec x, reusing the answer from a neighbouring question by mistake.
Losing the tan x term when simplifying e^(log|sec x + tan x|).

steps.label: Integrate and finish
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Expand (sec x + tan x)tan x and use sec²x − 1 = tan²x to integrate.
steps.memory_tip: sec x tan x integrates to sec x, and tan²x becomes sec²x − 1 before integrating.
lines: Hence the solution is y·(I.F.) = ∫(I.F.)Q dx
⇒ y(sec x + tan x) = ∫(sec x + tan x)tan x dx
= sec x + tan x − x + c

lines.text: y(sec x + tan x) = sec x + tan x − x + c

steps.why: Expanding the product (sec x + tan x)tan x gives two standard pieces: sec x tan x, whose antiderivative is sec x, and tan²x, which is rewritten as sec²x − 1 so it integrates to tan x − x.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the identity tan²x = sec²x − 1 and being unable to integrate tan²x directly.
Losing the −x term that comes from integrating the −1 inside sec²x − 1.
